title: The cost of reflection
sub: Invoke, delegates, Expression, UnsafeAccessor and Activator
cards/0/body:
Reflection is the API that hands you metadata as objects: Type, MethodInfo, PropertyInfo, FieldInfo. Through them you can find a member by name, read and write a value, call a method, create an object.

The cost has two parts. Lookup: GetMethod("WithTax") compares strings and checks BindingFlags. The call: the compiler does not know the types, so the arguments travel in an object[] and the runtime checks them on every call.
cards/0/deep:
The runtime caches MethodInfo objects inside the type, so a repeated GetMethod is cheaper than the first, but the string lookup and flag checks remain. How these caches and metadata tokens work is covered in the ".NET inside out" course.

typeof(Order) compiles to loading the type token and calling Type.GetTypeFromHandle; the JIT usually folds that into a constant.
cards/1/q: Shop.Order lives in Shop.dll, which is already loaded. Code in App.dll calls Type.GetType("Shop.Order"). What comes back?
cards/1/options/3: It depends on the assembly load order
cards/1/explain: Without an assembly name, Type.GetType searches only the calling assembly and System.Private.CoreLib. For a type from another assembly you need an assembly-qualified name: "Shop.Order, Shop". You get an exception only if you pass throwOnError: true.
cards/1/wrong/3: Whether Shop.dll is loaded does not matter: without an assembly name it is simply not searched.
cards/2/title: Five ways to call a method
cards/2/body:
Orders of magnitude for calling a small method on a typical x64 machine (exact numbers depend on the hardware and version — measure with BenchmarkDotNet):

  • a direct call — about a nanosecond or less: the JIT can inline the method;
  • UnsafeAccessor (.NET 8) — like a direct call, even to a private member;
  • a delegate from CreateDelegate or a compiled Expression — a few nanoseconds: an indirect call with no inlining;
  • MethodInfo.Invoke — tens of nanoseconds plus allocations on every call;
  • GetMethod + Invoke on every iteration — more still.

The gap is orders of magnitude, not percent. You notice it in a hot loop; for a couple of calls at startup you do not.
cards/3/q: Order from fastest to slowest. The method is small, everything is prepared in advance, the call is in a hot loop.
cards/3/items/3: GetMethod by name and Invoke on every iteration
cards/3/explain: The JIT can inline a direct call. A delegate is an indirect call. Invoke boxes arguments, allocates an array and checks types. A lookup by name adds string comparison on top.
cards/4/body:
On every MethodInfo.Invoke call:

  • an object[] is allocated for the arguments;
  • value-type arguments and the result are boxed;
  • the runtime checks the number and types of the arguments and the method's accessibility;
  • an exception from the method is wrapped in TargetInvocationException, the real one sits in InnerException.

None of this is needed when the signature is known in advance: then you use reflection once — to get a delegate.
cards/4/deep:
Since .NET 7, after the first calls the runtime generates an IL stub for the method, and Invoke became much faster than in .NET Framework. .NET 8 added MethodInvoker and ConstructorInvoker: arguments are passed without an object[], though value types are still boxed.

The BindingFlags.DoNotWrapExceptions flag turns the wrapping off: the method's exception propagates as is.
cards/5/q: The Pay method throws InvalidOperationException. What does this code print?
cards/5/explain: Invoke wraps the called method's exception in TargetInvocationException, so the first catch does not match. The original exception is in e.InnerException. To skip the wrapper, use BindingFlags.DoNotWrapExceptions.
cards/5/wrong/1: That is what a direct call would do. Invoke puts its own wrapper between you and the method.
cards/6/body:
If the signature is known at compile time, turn the MethodInfo into a delegate. You pay once, at creation; after that it is an ordinary delegate call: no array, no boxing, no checks.

An open delegate takes the instance as its first parameter: one delegate for all objects. A closed one is bound to a single object: m.CreateDelegate<Func<decimal, decimal>>(order).

A property is a pair of methods: build the delegate from p.GetMethod or p.SetMethod.
cards/6/deep:
The generic CreateDelegate<T>() arrived in .NET 5; before that you wrote (Func<…>)Delegate.CreateDelegate(typeof(Func<…>), m).

The delegate type must match the signature exactly, allowing for variance of reference types. For a struct method, an open delegate takes the instance by reference — you need your own delegate type with a ref parameter.
cards/7/q: Build a fast getter for the Total property
cards/7/explain: The getter is the get_Total method; its MethodInfo is in p.GetMethod. It takes an Order (an open delegate) and returns a decimal — that is Func<Order, decimal>. GetValue is the same slow path through object.
cards/8/title: Expression.Compile: when the types are known only at run time
cards/8/body:
A serializer or a mapper needs a getter for any property, and the type is known only at run time. Then a Func<object, object?> is built from an expression tree and compiled.

Compile() generates IL through DynamicMethod, and the JIT turns it into machine code. It is expensive: from hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds. But the call afterwards costs as much as a delegate call. So the result must be cached, for example by PropertyInfo.
cards/8/deep:
Where code cannot be generated at run time — Native AOT, iOS — Compile() does not fail; it returns a delegate over a tree interpreter. It works, but many times slower, and the win over Invoke is gone.

A value-type property is boxed when such a getter returns object — that is the price of the universal signature, not of reflection.
cards/9/body:
.NET 8 introduced [UnsafeAccessor]. You declare an extern static method, say which member it accesses, and the runtime generates the body itself. Kinds: Constructor, Method, StaticMethod, Field, StaticField.

The cost is that of a direct call: the JIT can inline it. The member is named statically, so it works with trimming and Native AOT.

Downsides: the name is a string. A typo surfaces on the first call as MissingFieldException or MissingMethodException. And you depend on private details of someone else's type — the next version may rename them.
cards/9/deep:
For a field the method returns a ref — you can both read and write. The first parameter is the instance (for static members too: its value is ignored, and its type says where to look).

.NET 9 added generics support: declare the method in a generic class with the same type parameters. .NET 10 added [UnsafeAccessorType] for when the type itself is not accessible at compile time.
cards/10/q: Match the approach with when you pay for it
cards/10/pairs/0/1: Allocations and checks on every call
cards/10/pairs/2/1: Expensive compilation, then a delegate-speed call
cards/10/pairs/3/1: Almost nothing: access like a direct call
cards/10/pairs/4/1: Looking up a member by string
cards/11/body:
Activator.CreateInstance(Type) creates an object with the parameterless constructor. For new T() in a generic method with the new() constraint the compiler emits a call to Activator.CreateInstance<T>() — there is no dedicated IL instruction for it.

In modern .NET the runtime caches the constructor it found, and the cost is close to a plain new plus a few nanoseconds. In .NET Framework the gap was much larger — hence the old advice to "cache a factory via Expression".

The expensive variant is CreateInstance(type, args) with arguments: matching a constructor by argument types, plus an array and boxing on every call.
cards/12/q: What does the compiler turn new T() into in Make<T>() where T : new()?
cards/12/options/3: A call to a static method T.New()
cards/12/explain: newobj needs a concrete constructor, and T has none until run time: for reference types the JIT even shares one body across all of them. So the compiler calls Activator.CreateInstance<T>(), which finds and caches the constructor of the actual type.
